evals.prompt: Write a Go function that reads a CSV file from a path and returns the rows as a slice of structs, with error handling.
evals.expected_output: Errors are wrapped with %w (not %v or a bare string); the file handle is closed via defer with the close error not silently dropped; declaration style and naming follow the house rules for the new code.
expectations: [deterministic] Wraps errors using %w in fmt.Errorf, not %v or a bare string, when returning an error from the file-open or parse path
[deterministic] Closes the file handle via a deferred Close call

[deterministic] Does not silently discard the error returned by a deferred Close on a handle that was written to - it captures the error into a named return, logs it, or wraps it. A bare deferred Close on a read-only handle is acceptable when the response says why it is safe there.
[deterministic] Uses explicit `var` declarations for variables outside any if/for/switch/select initializer expression (e.g. the slice of rows being built up), not `:=`
[deterministic] Does not use a grouped `var (...)` block anywhere; each `var` declaration is on its own line
[judgment] Chooses names whose descriptiveness scales with scope depth and complexity, avoiding one- and two-letter names outside the `ok`/`err` exceptions

evals.prompt: Write a table-driven test in Go for a function ValidateEmail(string) (bool, error).
evals.expected_output: Subtests via t.Run, a named test-case struct, and t.Parallel() where it is safe; declaration style and naming follow the house rules.
expectations: [deterministic] Runs each test case as a subtest via t.Run
[deterministic] Defines a named struct type for the test cases (e.g. `type testCase struct { ... }` or similarly named), rather than only an inline anonymous struct literal with no type name
[deterministic] Calls t.Parallel() inside the subtests
[deterministic] Uses explicit `var` declarations outside if/for/switch/select initializers and does not use a grouped `var (...)` block
[judgment] Field and variable names scale in descriptiveness with scope complexity, avoiding one- and two-letter names outside the `ok`/`err` exceptions

evals.prompt: Write a Go HTTP client method that POSTs a JSON payload and decodes the response, with a timeout.
evals.expected_output: The timeout is carried on a context.Context passed to http.NewRequestWithContext rather than only http.Client.Timeout; the response body is closed; the status code is checked before decoding.
expectations: [deterministic] Builds the request with http.NewRequestWithContext, passing a context.Context that carries the timeout (e.g. via context.WithTimeout), rather than relying only on http.Client.Timeout
[deterministic] Closes the response body via a deferred Close call
[deterministic] Checks the response status code before attempting to decode the response body
[deterministic] Wraps errors using %w in fmt.Errorf, not %v or a bare string
[judgment] Declaration style and naming in the new code follow the house rules (explicit var outside initializer expressions, no grouped var block, descriptive names scaled to scope)

evals.prompt: Write a Go worker pool that processes jobs from a channel with a bounded number of goroutines and collects errors.
evals.expected_output: Bounded goroutines, error collection that drops nothing under concurrency (errgroup or an explicit collector), and cancellation propagated by context so one failure stops the remaining work.
expectations: [deterministic] Bounds the number of concurrently running goroutines (e.g. a fixed worker count, a semaphore, or errgroup.SetLimit), rather than spawning one goroutine per job unbounded

[deterministic] Collects errors from workers without a data race or dropped error under concurrency, using errgroup.Group or an explicitly synchronized collector (mutex-protected slice or dedicated error channel drained by a single goroutine)

[deterministic] Propagates cancellation via context (e.g. context.WithCancel or errgroup's derived context) so that one worker's failure stops the remaining work rather than letting every job run to completion regardless
[judgment] Declaration style and naming in the new code follow the house rules

evals.prompt: Add structured logging to a Go HTTP service: set up the logger at startup and log each request with its method, path, and status.
evals.expected_output: Reaches for go.uber.org/zap with typed fields (zap.String, zap.Int, zap.Error) and an injected logger; does not reach for log/slog or the standard log package as the application logger, except log/slog confined to a bridge package or slog.LogValuer redaction role.
expectations: [deterministic] Imports and uses go.uber.org/zap as the logging library for the application's request logging
[deterministic] Uses typed field constructors (zap.String, zap.Int, and/or zap.Error) for the method, path, and status values rather than building the log line with fmt-style string formatting

[deterministic] Constructs the logger once at startup and passes/injects it into the request-handling code (e.g. via a struct field, middleware closure, or constructor parameter) rather than only a package-level global referenced directly inside the handler
[deterministic] Does not use the standard library log package as the application logger

[deterministic] If log/slog appears anywhere in the response, it appears only inside a bridge package (e.g. mentioning zapslog or an slog.Handler backed by zap) or an slog.LogValuer redaction implementation - never as the direct application logging call for the method/path/status line

evals.prompt: Write a Go function that parses a slice of "key=value" config strings into a map[string]string, returning an error for any malformed entry.
evals.expected_output: Declaration-style rule is followed: explicit var outside if/for/switch/select initializers, := confined to those initializers, no grouped var (...) block.
expectations: [deterministic] Declares the result map and any accumulator/loop-scoped variable that lives outside an if/for/switch/select initializer with an explicit `var`, not `:=`
[deterministic] Uses `:=` only as part of an initializer expression inside an if, for, switch, or select statement where the declared variable's scope is visibly limited to that statement
[deterministic] Does not use a grouped `var (...)` block anywhere in the function
[deterministic] Wraps the malformed-entry error using %w in fmt.Errorf, not %v or a bare string

evals.prompt: Write a Go function that, given a map[string][]int and a slice of candidate keys, returns the candidate whose slice has the largest sum, using nested loops to compute each sum. Skip any candidate that is not in the map; a candidate that is present with an empty slice counts, with a sum of zero.
evals.expected_output: Naming descriptiveness scales with nesting depth and complexity; one- and two-letter names are avoided outside the ok/err exceptions; declaration style is followed for the running best-key/best-sum state; absent candidates are detected with a comma-ok lookup rather than a nil or length check.
expectations: [deterministic] Declares the running best-key and best-sum tracking variables with explicit `var`, not `:=`, since they live outside any if/for/switch/select initializer

[deterministic] Detects an absent candidate with a comma-ok map lookup, not by comparing the looked-up slice to nil or checking its length (a nil comparison wrongly skips a present candidate stored with a nil slice, and a length check wrongly skips one stored with an empty slice), and names the boolean `ok` or a descriptive name such as `found`, never another one- or two-letter name

[judgment] Names inside the nested loop bodies grow more descriptive with nesting depth and complexity, avoiding one- and two-letter names other than the `ok`/`err` exceptions and idiomatic short-lived loop indices

evals.prompt: Looking at references/go-concurrency.md's errgroup example, explain why it writes `g, ctx := errgroup.WithContext(ctx)`, then write a new helper function of your own, in the same style, that runs a set of independent lookups concurrently and returns the first error.
evals.expected_output: Does not flag or rewrite the quoted reference-file example's `:=` usage as a house-style violation, since domain reference examples stay in upstream Go idiom by design; the new helper function it writes itself still follows the house declaration-style rule.
expectations: [judgment] Does not flag, apologize for, or rewrite the quoted `g, ctx := errgroup.WithContext(ctx)` example from the reference file as a declaration-style violation, treating it as upstream idiom the reference is allowed to keep

[judgment] Draws an explicit distinction between the reference file's own example and the new code it writes - naming the example as the reference's existing style and its own helper as house style - rather than applying one declaration style uniformly to both or passing over the difference in silence

[deterministic] In the new helper function it writes itself, uses explicit `var` for any declaration outside an if/for/switch/select initializer, rather than applying the reference example's `:=` style to its own new code

evals.prompt: This service's main.go already sets up `slog.New(slog.NewJSONHandler(os.Stdout, nil))` as its logger and passes it through the whole app - that's the project's existing, established logging decision. Add a log line inside the existing ProcessOrder function that records the order ID when processing starts, consistent with how the rest of the codebase already logs.
evals.expected_output: Where a project states its own logging decision, the project governs and the skill yields: the new log line uses the project's existing slog setup rather than introducing zap.
expectations: [deterministic] Uses slog (the project's existing established logger) for the new log line rather than introducing go.uber.org/zap
[deterministic] Does not introduce a second logging library alongside the project's existing slog setup
[judgment] States or otherwise makes clear that it is deferring to the project's already-established logging decision rather than applying the skill's default zap preference
